_about: Hand-curated 2026-11-14. Actions in the two new buckets (Continue, don't stop; Counsel and plan) and timing-specific actions not in the original draft. Each cites only sources read this session: guidance ids from guidance.json, 'label' = openFDA label text pulled by label_pull.py, PMIDs read in literature_read.json. basis: study | guidance | label | draft.
trigger_note: Heat-alert day = a local heat advisory, or CDC HeatRisk orange (moderate) or higher for people sensitive to heat. Team to confirm the NYC threshold.

all_classes.text: Run a pre-season medication review with the patient; document any hot-day changes and when to resume the usual schedule.
all_classes.note: WHO Europe p. 214; CDC/NYC general steps. In the Netherlands ~40% of medication-related AKI/dehydration admissions were judged preventable by timely adjustment (38831143).

all_classes.text: Ask about air conditioning and whether the patient can afford to run it; name a contact who will check on them; share cooling-centre and energy-assistance options.
Do not stop medicines abruptly on hot days without a plan from the prescriber.

Diuretics.text: Agree a hot-day fluid plan, including whether any fluid restriction should be relaxed.
Consider a lower summer dose where blood pressure is already at or below target; diuretics are the drugs doctors most often reduce in summer.
Check sodium and electrolytes in prolonged heat, especially in older adults.
Diuretics.who: Prescriber orders; nurse or pharmacist follows up

ACE inhibitors / ARBs.text: Avoid starting or adding a diuretic to an ACE inhibitor just before or during summer where it can wait; this combination carried the highest admission risk when started.
Monitor hydration; watch for vomiting, diarrhoea and low blood pressure.

Beta blockers.text: Do not stop a beta blocker abruptly in the heat (rebound risk); review the indication before summer instead.
Beta blockers.note: Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is standard label content; the label section was not pulled in this session.

Beta blockers.text: Tell patients that heart rate may not rise normally in heat, so a fitness watch's heart-rate warning can under-read strain.

Calcium channel blockers.text: Monitor hydration; watch for diarrhoea, vomiting and dizziness.

Anticholinergics.text: Deprescribe or switch where possible before summer (e.g. bladder antimuscarinics, sedating antihistamines).
Anticholinergics.note: Starting anticholinergic agents raised admission for dehydration or heat illness (27378245).

Anticholinergics.text: Warn that sweating is reduced: hot, dry skin and confusion are warning signs; a sweat or skin sensor will not show strain.

Antipsychotics.text: Do not stop abruptly; prioritise people on combination antipsychotic therapy for heat outreach.
Antipsychotics.note: BC 2021 heat dome: combination therapy OR 4.05 for death in schizophrenia.

Antipsychotics.text: Monitor electrolytes, temperature and signs of heat intolerance.

Lithium.text: Hydrate with water rather than electrolyte drinks; know the signs of lithium toxicity.

Antidepressants.text: Check sodium in older adults on SSRIs during prolonged heat.

Benzodiazepines / sedatives.text: Taper rather than stop; sedation dulls thirst, so add check-in calls on hot days.

Opioids.text: Offer naloxone and plan hot-day check-ins for people at risk of overdose.
Fentanyl patch: keep heating pads, electric blankets, hot tubs and direct sun off the patch; fever raises absorption.

Insulin.text: Keep unopened insulin refrigerated (2–8 °C); in-use pens and vials up to 30 °C for 28 days; keep out of hot cars; plan for power cuts.
Check glucose more often in heat (CGM if available); warm skin at the injection or pump site speeds absorption.

SGLT2 inhibitors.text: Sick-day rule: pause when unable to eat or drink, vomiting or dehydrated (volume depletion, ketoacidosis).
SGLT2 inhibitors.who: Prescriber sets the plan; pharmacist reinforces
SGLT2 inhibitors.note: Labels warn about volume depletion; dehydration adverse events peak in July–August (Japan).

Metformin and sulfonylureas.text: Sulfonylureas: check glucose more often on hot days; hypoglycaemia rises with temperature for glimepiride and glyburide.

NSAIDs.text: Avoid NSAIDs when dehydrated, especially with a diuretic plus ACE inhibitor/ARB; do not self-medicate with NSAIDs after heat exposure.

Topiramate / zonisamide.text: Warn families that children may sweat less: limit exertion in heat and watch for fever.

Stimulants.text: Warn about overheating during sport in hot weather; core temperature can rise without feeling harder.

Heat-labile emergency products.text: Keep inhalers, auto-injectors and GTN out of hot cars and direct sun; inhaler canisters can burst above 49 °C (120 °F).
Heat-labile emergency products.note: Epinephrine and fentanyl stayed within specification for a year in an ambulance (35717271): replacement after brief heat exposure may not always be needed.

GLP-1 agonists.text: Consider pausing when vomiting or unable to keep fluids down; check kidney function if losses persist.

Parkinson / dopaminergic.text: Never stop or sharply cut dopaminergic drugs in the heat: withdrawal can cause hyperthermia.

Cholinesterase inhibitors.text: Rivastigmine patch: keep saunas and strong sun off the patch; carers check fluids on hot days.

Combination: diuretic + ACEi/ARB (± NSAI.text: Avoid starting the ACEi + diuretic combination just before or during summer when it can wait; flag any NSAID added on top.

Polypharmacy (several heat-sensitising d.text: Put people on several heat-sensitising drugs (plus age 65+, no AC or living alone) on the pre-season review and heat outreach list.
